title: Colleagues Who Agree and Then Run a Different Play
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Addresses colleagues who agree in bad faith -- consenting to a plan to avoid conflict, then quietly pursuing their own path -- and why goodwill-based accountability rarely corrects the pattern. Notes that confronted colleagues often deny, deflect, or claim they followed the 'spirit' of the agreement, which erodes trust over time. Since manipulative compliance doesn't respond to clarity alone, the piece recommends imposing structure: written documentation with names attached, distributed publicly, requiring initial action steps as proof of commitment, and demanding written rationale for any change in direction.
points: Bad-faith agreement -- consenting to avoid conflict, then reneging -- is a pattern best addressed with structure, not just clearer conversations.
Public, written documentation of an agreement functions as a strong constraint against later deviation, more so than private clarity.
Structure controls the behavior but doesn't repair the trust already lost -- dealing with a chronically bad-faith colleague remains exhausting even when contained.
quotes: The thought occurs that this passive resistance is intentional. They comply, falsely, to remove any obstacles, and then do what they please.
When confronted after the fact, they often play stupid, pretending they didn’t understand what they agreed to or claim they didn’t believe the decision was final.
Highly manipulative behavior, like passive resistance or selective compliance, is best quashed by structure.
Articulating the agreement in writing with their name attached and distributing it to a broader group of colleagues and leaders normally constitutes a strong constraint.
Another idea is to insist on a written rationale for any change in direction. This requirement often inhibits rogue behavior after a tepid agreement.
Sadly, structure controls bad behavior, but it doesn’t change character. The good news is that visible processes typically outmaneuver hidden agendas.
